What do variance and normality tests establish?

Source: vignettes/variance-normality-tests.Rmd
variance-normality-tests.Rmd

Do formal tests support the concerns in a braking-distance residual plot? We will use the same model as the residual diagnostics guide, distinguish two null hypotheses and interpret the results together. Here both the variance test and normality checks give evidence against their nulls. They identify questions for further investigation, without choosing a remedy.

Keep the model and observations fixed

Example data: R’s built-in cars dataset

The 50 historic observations record speed in miles per hour and stopping distance in feet. All measurements are present. The earlier plots showed wider residual spread at higher fitted distances and an upper tail that bends above the normal Q-Q line. Fit exactly the same straight-line model so that the tests address those findings.

library(olsrr)
braking_data <- datasets::cars
stopifnot(nrow(braking_data) == 50L, !anyNA(braking_data))
braking_model <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = braking_data)

The assumptions concern unobserved model errors conditional on speed. The functions use fitted residuals to investigate them. Residuals inherit constraints and dependence from fitting, so formal distribution tests applied to them are diagnostic approximations, not a complete validation of the error model.

Test a specified variance pattern

The Breusch-Pagan null is constant conditional error variance. The default call looks for variance associated with the model’s fitted values. Its alternative concerns that specified direction; it does not cover every possible pattern of changing variance. This implementation assumes normal errors for its reference calibration, as well as an appropriate mean model and independent observations.

variance_test <- ols_test_breusch_pagan(braking_model)
variance_test
#> 
#>  Breusch Pagan Test for Heteroskedasticity
#>  -----------------------------------------
#>  Ho: the variance is constant            
#>  Ha: the variance is not constant        
#> 
#>               Data               
#>  --------------------------------
#>  Response : dist 
#>  Variables: fitted values of dist 
#> 
#>        Test Summary         
#>  ---------------------------
#>  DF            =    1 
#>  Chi2          =    4.650233 
#>  Prob > Chi2   =    0.0310

The chi-square statistic is 4.650 with one degree of freedom and p = 0.0310. At a prespecified 5% significance level, that is evidence against the constant-variance null in the tested direction. It agrees with the visual concern about widening spread, but does not prove which variance function is correct. An incorrect mean model can also create a residual pattern.

Changing variance does not by itself make OLS coefficients biased: unbiasedness requires a correctly specified conditional mean with zero conditional-mean errors, and consistency needs corresponding exogeneity and regularity conditions. The usual constant-variance standard errors can nevertheless be inappropriate, affecting confidence intervals and tests. A rejected variance test does not invalidate every fitted value or automatically select weighted fitting, a transformation or another remedy.

Ask a separate normality question

Each normality check has a normal-distribution null, with location and scale estimated from the data. They emphasize different kinds of departure and inspect the same residuals, so their results are not four independent confirmations. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov row uses the Lilliefors correction for estimating the normal mean and standard deviation.

normality_tests <- ols_test_normality(braking_model)
normality_tests
#> ------------------------------------------------------------
#>              Test                    Statistic       pvalue  
#> ------------------------------------------------------------
#> Shapiro-Wilk                           0.9451         0.0215 
#> Kolmogorov-Smirnov (Lilliefors)        0.1296         0.0353 
#> Cramer-von Mises                       0.1257         0.0483 
#> Anderson-Darling                       0.7941         0.0369 
#> ------------------------------------------------------------

The Shapiro-Wilk p-value is 0.0215; the Lilliefors, Cramer-von Mises and Anderson-Darling p-values are 0.0353, 0.0483 and 0.0369. These results indicate departures from a normal shape at a 5% threshold, consistent with the Q-Q plot’s upper tail. They do not distinguish skewness caused by changing variance from a missed mean relationship or unusual observations.

A large p-value would mean insufficient evidence against the particular null, not proof that an assumption holds. Small samples can miss relevant departures and large samples can detect minor ones. Normality is useful for exact small-sample inference under the model; it is not necessary just to compute least-squares coefficients. No test here establishes independence or the suitability of the model for new vehicles.

Keep other test options in context

Question or option Function and scope
Test variance against model predictors or selected predictors ols_test_breusch_pagan() with rhs = TRUE or vars
Test several variance directions multiple = TRUE with rhs = TRUE; p.adj offers Holm, Bonferroni and Sidak adjustments
Explore another variance test ols_test_score(), ols_test_f(); read their assumptions before use
Summarize alignment with normal scores ols_test_correlation(); this is not a serial-correlation diagnostic

These options change the question or calibration. Do not search among them for a favorable p-value. The variance and residual-normality diagnostics used here are not supported for weighted models; consult the individual function help before extending the example.

Separate sidebar: compare genuinely grouped variances

Example data: R’s built-in PlantGrowth dataset

Bartlett’s test asks whether population variances are equal across groups. Here dried plant weights have 10 observations in each of three groups: a control and two treatments. The dataset documentation does not specify the weight unit. This is a separate grouped question, not a replacement test of the cars regression’s residual variance.

ols_test_bartlett(datasets::PlantGrowth, "weight", group_var = "group")
#> 
#>     Bartlett's Test of Homogenity of Variances    
#> ------------------------------------------------
#> Ho: Variances are equal across groups
#> Ha: Variances are unequal for atleast two groups
#> 
#>        Test Summary         
#>  ---------------------------
#>  DF            =    2 
#>  Chi2          =    2.878574 
#>  Prob > Chi2   =    0.2371

The statistic is 2.879 on two degrees of freedom, with p = 0.2371. There is insufficient evidence against equal group variances; equality is not established. Bartlett’s calibration is sensitive to departures from normality and assumes independent observations within and between groups. Group distributions deserve inspection before relying on it.

Next, revisit the two residual plots and investigate the mean shape and spread together. The help pages for ols_test_breusch_pagan(), ols_test_normality() and ols_test_bartlett() describe their interfaces and limitations. Choose any follow-up model using the data context and compare its diagnostics on the same rows.
